Roofs we work on.

Every roof is built a little differently. Pick yours to see how it is laid and what usually goes wrong with it.

Run your pointer over the roof

Clay and concrete tiles

The most common roof in the area. Each tile hangs on a timber batten by its nibs, and some or all are nailed or clipped, depending on its age.

  • Usually goes wrong: slipped or cracked tiles, a loose ridge, perished mortar at the verges.
  • What we do: match and replace tiles, re-bed or dry-fix ridges, re-tile a slope or the whole roof.
Ask about a tiled roof

Natural slate

Thin split slates, each held by two nails or a hook, laid so every joint is covered by the slate above.

  • Usually goes wrong: nails rust through and slates slide down, called nail sickness, and old slates crack.
  • What we do: refix slipped slates with tingles or hooks, replace with matched slate, re-slate when too many have gone.
Ask about a slate roof

Stone slate

Heavy limestone slates laid in diminishing courses: the biggest at the eaves, getting smaller towards the ridge.

  • Usually goes wrong: oak pegs rot, battens give way, moss holds water, slates slip in groups.
  • What we do: sort, re-peg and re-lay sound slates, top up with reclaimed stone of the same size and colour.
Ask about a stone slate roof

Flat roofs

Extensions, garages and dormers, covered in felt, rubber (EPDM) or fibreglass (GRP) over a timber deck.

  • Usually goes wrong: ponding water, splits at the edges, blisters, failed upstands against a wall.
  • What we do: patch where it is sound, or strip and re-cover with a new deck and better falls.
Ask about a flat roof

Lead and metal

Flashings, valleys, bays and porches, dressed by hand so water runs past every join.

  • Usually goes wrong: splits from pieces that were too long, lifted flashings, theft, old soldered patches.
  • What we do: renew lead in the right sizes and codes, re-dress and re-point flashings, line valleys and gutters.
Ask about leadwork

Older and listed roofs

Handmade clay, old peg tiles and lime mortar. Repairs keep as much of the old roof as possible.

  • Usually goes wrong: soft handmade tiles flake, lime pointing washes out, hidden timbers decay.
  • What we do: reuse what is sound, source matching reclaimed materials, and work with your conservation officer where needed.
Ask about an older roof

What one slipped slate does.

  1. It starts with one slate. A calm evening. The roof has kept the rain out for years, but one nail has quietly rusted through.
  2. A storm lifts it. Wind gets under the loose slate and it slides out. From the ground you might never notice.
  3. Water finds the gap. Rain runs in, along the felt and the timbers, and shows up as a stain somewhere else.
  4. Get in touch as soon as you see it. Put a bucket under the drip and call or send the form straight away. While it is one slate and a damp patch, it is a small job.
  5. We look first, then talk it through. We check the ceiling and the roof, take photos, and show you what we found, the fix and the price before any work starts.
  6. Then we put it right. The slate goes back, the rest of the roof is checked, and the ceiling dries out. Tell us what you have spotted

Where a roof lets water in.

Six places roofs fail. Most leaks start at one of them. Scroll to walk round the roof: each stop shows where water gets in, what you would notice inside, and the usual fix.

Stop 1 of 6

1 2 3 4 5 6 Ridge
  1. 1Ridge. Cracked mortar or loose ridge tiles let wind-driven rain in at the top.You might notice: damp in the loft along the ridge, or a patch on a top-floor ceiling. Usual fix: re-bed or dry-fix the ridge tiles. Sounds like mine: ridge
  2. 2Chimney stack. Crumbling pointing and a cracked top let rain soak down through the brickwork.You might notice: damp on the chimney breast, or stains round the fireplace. Usual fix: repoint the stack, renew the flaunching or fit a cap. Sounds like mine: chimney stack
  3. 3Lead flashing. Lifted or split flashing where the roof meets a chimney or wall lets water run straight in.You might notice: damp inside where the roof meets a wall, often after wind-driven rain. Usual fix: re-dress or renew the lead and repoint the joint. Sounds like mine: lead flashing
  4. 4Valley. Where two slopes meet, a worn lining or a blocked channel spills water into the timbers.You might notice: damp in the corner of a ceiling below where two roofs meet. Usual fix: clear the valley, or reline it in new lead. Sounds like mine: valley
  5. 5Eaves. Slipped tiles or slates and worn underlay at the bottom edge soak the fascia and the top of the wall.You might notice: damp on the tops of outside walls, and fascia boards going soft. Usual fix: refix the bottom courses and renew the felt at the eaves. Sounds like mine: eaves
  6. 6Gutter. A blocked or sagging gutter overflows and sends water down the wall.You might notice: damp on one outside wall, with green streaks below the gutter. Usual fix: clear, realign or replace the gutter. Sounds like mine: gutter

From first look to handover.

Four steps, always in this order, so you know what happens next.

  1. 01

    Inspect

    A look at the roof from a ladder or scaffold, then into the loft. Slates, ridge, valleys, flashings and gutters are checked and photographed.

  2. 02

    Quote

    A written quote that names the fault, the fix and the materials, and lists what is left out so nothing arrives as a surprise.

  3. 03

    Work

    The agreed work, done as quoted. On a re-roof, old tiles come off and new battens, underlay and tiles go on, planned so the roof is never left open overnight.

    If something new is uncovered, it is explained before any extra work is added.

  4. 04

    Handover

    Gutters and drive are cleared and you walk round the roof from the ground. Photos of the finished work follow.

Tell us about your roof

Looking after your roof.

A few minutes each season, mostly from the ground, heads off many of the repairs we see. Here is what to look for and when.

Autumn

  • Clear leaves out of gutters, valleys and downpipe tops.
  • Look for slipped or cracked tiles before the winter storms.
  • Check the lead and pointing round the chimney.
  • Cut back branches that touch or overhang the roof.

Winter

  • After a storm, look for tiles or slates on the ground.
  • Watch ceilings and the tops of walls for new damp patches.
  • Drips in the loft on frosty mornings are often condensation, not a leak.
  • Never go up on a wet or icy roof. Call us instead.

Spring

  • Look for moss and lichen building up on the tiles.
  • Check gutters once nesting birds have moved on.
  • Look along the ridge and verges for loose or missing mortar.
  • Plan bigger jobs for the drier months.

Summer

  • Settled weather is the best time for re-roofing and bigger repairs.
  • Check flat roofs for blisters and cracks after hot spells.
  • Clean or repaint fascias and soffits.
  • Have a survey done while it is easy to see everything.

Roofing advice.

Short, honest guides for homeowners. No ladders needed for any of them.

  • Checking your roof from the ground 3 minute read

    Stand back on the pavement or at the end of the garden, ideally with binoculars, on a bright day.

    • Look for gaps or lines of tiles that are not straight.
    • Check the ridge for missing or loose ridge tiles.
    • Look at the lead and pointing where the roof meets the chimney.
    • Follow the gutters: sagging, plants growing or water stains below a joint all mean a blockage or a leak.

    Take photos as you go. They help us more than you might think.

  • After a storm: what to look for 2 minute read

    Wait until the wind has dropped. Then, from the ground:

    • Look for tiles, slates or ridge pieces on the ground or in the gutter.
    • Check the loft with a torch for daylight or wet patches.
    • Photograph any damage for your insurer before anything is moved.
    • If water is coming in, put a bucket under it, move electrics away and call us.
  • Moss on the roof: when it matters 2 minute read

    A little moss is mostly cosmetic. It starts to matter when:

    • It is thick enough to lift the edges of tiles.
    • It washes down and blocks gutters and downpipes.
    • It sits in valleys and holds water against the lead.

    Avoid pressure washing: it can strip the surface off older tiles and force water underneath. Gentle hand removal and a treatment last longer.

Open a question to see it drawn.

Roofs sometimes hide rotten battens or a failed valley once the tiles are off. We stop, show you photos, explain the options and agree the cost in writing before any extra work starts.

A few slates or a section of ridge is usually a few hours to a day. A full re-roof on an average house is more often one to two weeks, depending on size and weather.

Beyond a small repair at low level, scaffolding is normally needed for safe access. It is often the largest single line on a roofing quote, so check whether it is listed separately.

Roofing stops in heavy rain, high wind and frost, because wet slates are unsafe underfoot and some materials will not bond. Expect dates to move with the forecast.

Yes. The workmanship guarantee is written on the invoice, with what it covers and for how long. New tiles and slates also carry the manufacturer's guarantee. Ask to see the terms before you agree a quote.
